origin: A pictograph of a person seen from the side, with a head, a body and two legs. It is one of the oldest and simplest characters, already clear in oracle-bone script.
culture: 人 is the root of words like 人们 (people) and 人生 (life). Confucian thought places 人 at the center of the world, and the virtue 仁 (benevolence) combines 人 with 二 — 'person among two', i.e. how we treat others.

origin: A pictograph of an open mouth. The square shape simply outlines the lips.
culture: 口 appears in words for entrances and openings (门口, door). Measuring family size as 几口人 — 'how many mouths' — reflects an agrarian society where each mouth had to be fed.

origin: A pictograph of a hand with five fingers; the modern form keeps three 'fingers' and a wrist stroke.
culture: As the radical 扌it marks verbs done with the hands: 打 (hit), 找 (find), 拿 (take). 手机, 'hand machine', is the everyday word for mobile phone.

origin: A pictograph of the sun — a circle with a dot in the middle, squared off over time into today's rectangle with one line.
culture: 日 means both 'sun' and 'day', so dates use it (五日, the 5th). Together with 月 it forms 明, 'bright'. Japan is 日本, 'sun origin' — the land where the sun rises.

origin: A pictograph of a crescent moon. Ancient forms drew the moon with two inner strokes, later simplified to the modern shape.
culture: 月 means both 'moon' and 'month' — the lunar cycle defined the traditional Chinese calendar. The Mid-Autumn Festival celebrates the full moon with mooncakes, and poets have sung to the moon for three thousand years.

origin: A pictograph of three mountain peaks rising from a base line.
culture: Mountains are sacred in Chinese culture — the Five Great Mountains (五岳) were pilgrimage sites for emperors. 山水画, 'mountain-water painting', is the highest genre of Chinese landscape art.
examples: 上山 shàngshān — to go up the mountain

origin: A pictograph of flowing water — a central current with splashes or rivulets on both sides.
culture: Water is one of the five elements (五行). Laozi praised water as the highest good: it benefits everything yet contends with nothing. The radical 氵('three drops of water') marks liquid-related characters like 河 and 海.

origin: A pictograph of a rising flame with sparks on either side.
culture: Fire is one of the five elements, linked to summer and the south. 火车 'fire cart' is a train, and 火锅 'fire pot' is the beloved hotpot meal shared around a bubbling broth.

origin: A pictograph of a tree: trunk, branches reaching up, roots spreading down.
culture: 木 doubles for 'wood' and appears doubled as 林 (forest) and tripled as 森 (dense forest). It is one of the five elements, associated with spring and growth.

origin: A pictograph of a woman kneeling with arms crossed in front — a posture of grace in ancient times.
culture: 女 combines with 子 (child) to make 好 'good'. Chinese traditionally says 女儿 'female child' for daughter. The goddess Nüwa (女娲) is said to have created humanity from clay.

origin: A pictograph of a baby with a large head, a body and two arms, wrapped so the legs show as one stroke.
culture: 子 meant 'child' and also became an honorific for masters — 孔子 (Confucius) is 'Master Kong'. Today it is the most common noun suffix: 桌子 (table), 椅子 (chair), 孩子 (child).

origin: An ideograph combining 女 (woman) and 子 (child): a mother with her child was the ancient picture of everything 'good'.
culture: 好 is probably the first word every learner masters — 你好, 'you good', means hello. Chinese well-wishing revolves around 好: 好运 good luck, 好事 good things, 好人 a good person.

origin: An ideograph of 日 (sun) and 月 (moon) together — the two brightest things in the sky combine to mean 'bright'.
culture: 明 gives us 明天 'bright day' = tomorrow, and 明白 'bright and clear' = to understand. The Ming dynasty (明朝, 1368–1644) took its name from this shining character.

origin: An ideograph: 人 (person) leaning against 木 (tree) — a person resting in the shade of a tree means 'to rest'.
culture: 休息, 'to rest', is a word Chinese people use warmly: 好好休息 'rest well' is standard care-talk to anyone tired or sick. The image of pausing under a tree fits the Daoist ideal of unforced ease.

origin: An ideograph: 宀 (roof) over 豕 (pig). A house with livestock under the roof was the ancient picture of a household.
culture: 家 means both 'home' and 'family' — in Chinese the two are one idea. The family is the core unit of society, and 大家 'big family' came to mean 'everybody'. 国家 'country' is literally 'state-family'.
examples: 回家 huí jiā — to go home

origin: An ideograph: 女 (woman) under 宀 (roof) — a woman at home meant 'peace' and 'safety'.
culture: 安 is the character of blessings: 平安 'safe and sound' is the most heartfelt wish for travelers. Xi'an (西安) is 'Western Peace'. 晚安 'night peace' is how you say good night.
examples: 平安 píng'ān — safe and sound

origin: An ideograph: 子 (child) under 宀 (roof) — originally 'to raise children at home', extended to the 'children' of spoken words: written characters.
culture: Chinese calligraphy treats each 字 as a work of art. Children once learned writing on 字帖 copybooks, and 'a person's writing shows the person' (字如其人) is a common saying.

origin: The traditional form 學 shows two hands arranging 爻 (divination lines) over a 子 (child) under a roof — a child being taught.
culture: Learning is the supreme Confucian virtue; the Analects open with 'To learn and practice in due time — is this not a joy?' (学而时习之，不亦说乎). 学习 'study-practice' keeps that pairing.

origin: A phono-semantic compound: 氵(water) gives the meaning (the Han River), and the right side gives the sound. It named the Han dynasty, then the Han people and their language.
culture: Over 90% of Chinese are 汉族 Han Chinese, named after the great Han dynasty (206 BC–220 AD). 汉字 'Han characters' and 汉语 'Han language' carry the dynasty's name to this day.

origin: A phono-semantic compound: 讠(speech radical) shows it relates to language, and 吾 gives the sound.
culture: The speech radical 讠(言) marks hundreds of language words: 说 speak, 话 talk, 读 read, 谢谢 thank. 语言 'language' and 语法 'grammar' are built on it.

origin: A pictograph of a vertical line piercing the center of a rectangle — an arrow hitting the middle of a target, or a flagpole in the middle of a settlement.
culture: 中国, the 'Middle Kingdom' or 'Central State', reflects the ancient view of China as the center of the civilized world. 中 also means 'to hit the mark', as in 打中.

origin: The traditional 國 shows 或 (territory) inside 囗 (enclosure/walls). The simplified form puts 玉 (jade) — a treasure — inside the walls.
culture: 国 pairs with 家 (family) to make 国家 'country' — the state as an extension of the family. 国庆, National Day on October 1st, fills streets with flags and the character 国.

origin: The character shows 艹 (grass/plant) over 人 and 木 — a person among plants picking leaves. It split off from an older character 荼 in the Tang dynasty.
culture: Tea was discovered in China, where legend credits Emperor Shennong around 2737 BC. 喝茶 is a way of life: guests are always offered tea, and 茶馆 teahouses are social living rooms.
examples: 喝茶 hē chá — to drink tea

origin: A phono-semantic compound: 饣(food radical) marks it as food, 反 gives the sound. It means cooked rice — and by extension any meal.
culture: Rice is so central that 吃饭 'eat rice' simply means 'to eat a meal'. The daily greeting 你吃饭了吗？ 'Have you eaten?' is the Chinese 'How are you?'.

origin: A pictograph of a fish with a head, scaly body and tail — the tail fins became the bottom four dots, simplified to a single line.
culture: Fish 鱼 yú sounds exactly like 余 'surplus', so a whole fish is essential at New Year's dinner: 年年有余 'may every year bring surplus'. Fish are never flipped over when eating — fishermen fear a 'capsized boat'.
examples: 吃鱼 chī yú — to eat fish

origin: A pictograph of a horse with mane, four legs and tail, rotated upright over time.
culture: The horse is one of the twelve zodiac animals and a symbol of speed and success: 马上 'on horseback' now just means 'right away'. Horse motifs gallop through Chinese art from Han tomb figures to Xu Beihong's ink paintings.

origin: A pictograph of a cow's head seen from the front: two horns and ears.
culture: Oxen plowed China's fields for millennia, so 牛 came to mean 'awesome' in slang. The Ox is the second zodiac animal, standing for diligence, and 牛奶 'cow milk' is everyday vocabulary.

origin: A pictograph of a sheep's head with curving horns, eyes and nose flattened into horizontal lines.
culture: Sheep were ancient sacrifices, so 羊 sits inside 美 'beautiful' (big sheep) and 善 'good'. The Goat/Ram is the eighth zodiac sign, associated with gentleness.

origin: A pictograph of a person standing with arms stretched wide — 'big' as a person at full span.
culture: 大 pairs with 小 in one of the first antonym sets learners meet. 大家 'big family' means everyone, and 大学 'big learning' is a university.

origin: A pictograph of three small dots or grains — little things scattered — drawn as a stroke with two side dots.
culture: 小 is used affectionately before surnames: 小王 'Little Wang' for a younger friend. 小姐 'little elder-sister' means Miss, and 小心 'small heart' means 'be careful'.

origin: An ideograph: a short stroke above a horizontal baseline — 'above'.
culture: 上/下 structure countless pairs: 上午/下午 (morning/afternoon), 上面/下面 (top/bottom), 上学 (go to school), 上班 (start work). It also means 'previous', as in 上个星期 last week.
examples: 上班 shàngbān — to go to work

origin: An ideograph: a short stroke below a horizontal baseline — 'below'.
culture: 下 means 'down' but also 'next': 下星期 is next week. 下雨 'the sky sends down rain' is the everyday way to say it rains, and 坐下 'sit down' is the first classroom command learners hear.

origin: A pictograph of the human heart, showing the organ's chambers and vessels.
culture: Chinese tradition locates thinking in the heart, not the brain, so the heart radical 忄marks emotion words: 想 think, 快 fast/快乐 happy, 忙 busy (a 'lost' heart), 爱 love.

origin: A pictograph of a double door with two swinging panels — the simplified form keeps one panel and its hinge.
culture: Doors guard Chinese homes: red couplets are pasted on them at New Year, and door gods (门神) protect households. 门口 'door-mouth' is the doorway, and 开门大吉 wishes business success.
examples: 开门 kāimén — to open the door

origin: A pictograph of a chariot seen from above: a box with two wheels on an axle, simplified to its modern cross-and-frame.
culture: 车 heads a family of modern transport words: 火车 train (fire-cart), 汽车 car (steam-cart), 自行车 bicycle (self-moving cart), 出租车 taxi (out-rent cart).

origin: A pictograph of grains of rice scattered around a central stalk or threshing frame.
culture: Rice shaped Chinese civilization; 米饭 is the heart of a southern meal. 米 also loans its sound to 'meter' (米), and 米酒 rice wine flows at festivals.

origin: A pictograph of a cowrie shell — shells were ancient China's earliest money.
culture: Because cowries were currency, the shell radical 贝 marks money words: 贵 expensive, 买/卖 buy/sell (traditional 買/賣), 财 wealth, 账 account. You can read Chinese economic history in its characters.

origin: A pictograph of an eye 目 on top of a person 儿 — the eye personified means 'to see'.
culture: 见 lives in goodbyes: 再见 'again-see' is 'see you again', and 明天见 is 'see you tomorrow'. 见面 'see face' means to meet in person.

origin: A pictograph of an elderly person with long hair leaning on a cane — 'old'.
culture: Respect for elders is a Confucian cornerstone, so 老 is honorific: 老师 'old master' is teacher, 老王 'Old Wang' is a warm way to address a friend, and 老人 are venerated on the Double Ninth Festival.

origin: Two strings of cowrie shells tied together — a unit of money — later read as two moons 月 side by side and borrowed for 'companion'.
culture: Confucius celebrated 有朋自远方来 'friends coming from afar'. The character's doubled form suggests companions standing side by side — 朋友 'friend' doubles it again with 友.
examples: 好朋友 hǎo péngyou — good friend

origin: A pictograph of two right hands reaching in the same direction — hands joined in help mean 'friend'.
culture: 友 appears in 友好 'friendly' and 友谊 'friendship', a word China uses in diplomacy: 友谊商店 'Friendship Stores' once served foreign visitors.

origin: The traditional 愛 shows 心 (heart) in the middle with a hand above and a foot below — the heart moved to act. The simplified form replaces the heart with 友 (friend).
culture: 爱 covers love of people, food and hobbies alike: 我爱你是 'I love you', 爱吃 is 'love to eat'. The 2008 Beijing Olympics theme 'One World, One Dream' used 同一个世界，同一个梦想 — love as unity.

origin: A phono-semantic compound: 礻(altar/spirit radical) plus a right side picturing a full wine jar — offerings at the altar brought 'blessing'.
culture: 福 is the luckiest character in China. At New Year people paste it upside down (福倒了) because 'upside down' 倒 sounds like 'arrive' 到 — 'fortune has arrived'.
examples: 祝福 zhùfú — to wish well

origin: A pictograph of a horned, whiskered serpent-like creature rearing up — the dragon, simplified from 龍.
culture: Unlike Western dragons, the Chinese 龙 is benevolent — ruler of water and rain, symbol of the emperor and of China itself. People proudly call themselves 龙的传人 'descendants of the dragon'.
examples: 龙年 lóngnián — Year of the Dragon

origin: A pictograph of a person 人 carrying ripe grain 禾 on their back — the harvest, which came once a year.
culture: The New Year monster 年 was scared away by red and firecrackers, the legend says — hence red decorations and fireworks. 过年 'pass the year' is to celebrate Spring Festival.

origin: The traditional 書 shows a hand holding a brush 聿 over 曰 — writing things down. The simplified form keeps the flourish of quick cursive.
culture: Books were bamboo slips tied with cords before paper was invented in Han China. Calligraphy 书法 — 'the way of writing' — remains one of the highest arts, practiced with brush, ink, paper and inkstone.

origin: A phono-semantic compound: 广 (shelter/building radical) over 占 which gives the sound — a building where goods are kept.
culture: 店 pairs with 商 to make 商店 'shop'. Old Chinese inns (客店) hung lanterns with the character 店 outside, and story-tellers set countless wuxia scenes in roadside inns.

origin: A phono-semantic compound: 钅(metal radical) marks it as metal/coin, 戋 gives the sound. Early coins were cast bronze 'spades' and 'knives'.
culture: Round coins with square holes — 铜钱 — circulated for two thousand years; the square hole let them be strung like beads. 红包 'red envelopes' of gift money are essential at New Year and weddings.
examples: 多少钱 duōshao qián — how much

origin: A pictograph: the top line is the sky, below it a cloud, and four dots of falling rain.
culture: Rain decides harvests, so ancient kings performed rain dances. 下雨 uses 下 'down' — rain 'comes down'. In the solar terms, 雨水 'Rain Water' (mid-February) marks the spring thaw.

origin: A pictograph of a lightning bolt branching through a rain field 申 — 'lightning'. Modern inventions recycled it for all things electric.
culture: 电 became the building block of modern vocabulary: 电话 'electric talk' telephone, 电视 'electric vision' TV, 电脑 'electric brain' computer, 电影 'electric shadows' movies.

origin: A pictograph of vapor or breath rising in three curling strokes — steam, air, breath.
culture: 气 qì is a cornerstone concept: the vital energy flowing through body and world, cultivated in qigong 气功 and read by feng shui 风水. 天气 'heaven's qi' is simply the weather.

origin: A pictograph of a person 大 with the head emphasized by a horizontal stroke — the sky above man.
culture: 天 means 'sky', 'day' and 'heaven' at once. Emperors ruled by the 天命 'Mandate of Heaven', and Beijing's 天坛 Temple of Heaven was where they prayed for harvests.

origin: A phono-semantic compound: 土 (earth radical) gives the meaning, 也 gives the sound — 'ground, earth'.
culture: 地 pairs with 天 as the cosmic duo 天地 'heaven and earth'. In the classic 三字经 primer, 三才者，天地人 names the 'three powers': heaven, earth and humankind.

origin: A pictograph of several shining dots in the sky, later given 日 (sun) on top and 生 (birth/sound) below — 'stars'.
culture: Chinese astronomers mapped the stars into the 28 lunar mansions two millennia ago. The Weaver Girl and Cowherd stars (织女/牛郎) meet once a year on the Qixi festival — Chinese Valentine's Day. 星期 'star period' means week.

origin: A pictograph of fruit 田-like shapes growing on a tree 木.
culture: 果 means 'fruit' and also 'result' — what a tree bears. 水果 'water fruit' is the everyday word for fruit, served after nearly every Chinese meal.

origin: A phono-semantic compound: 艹 (plant radical) over 采 (to pick) — 'picked plants', i.e. vegetables or dishes.
culture: 菜 means both 'vegetable' and a cooked 'dish': 点菜 is to order food. Chinese cuisine divides into Eight Great Cuisines (八大菜系), from spicy Sichuan to delicate Cantonese.
examples: 点菜 diǎn cài — to order dishes

origin: A pictograph of a hanging cut of meat with marbling strokes inside.
culture: As the radical 月 (the 'meat moon') it hides in body words: 脸 face, 腿 leg, 脑 brain. 羊肉 mutton warms northern winters, and 肉夹馍 is Xi'an's beloved 'Chinese hamburger'.

origin: The traditional 醫 contains 殳 (a weapon/tool), 酉 (wine jug, i.e. medicine) and 匸 (a box) — arrows removed, wounds treated with spirits.
culture: Traditional Chinese medicine (中医) has treated patients for over two thousand years with herbs, acupuncture and pulse reading. 医生 'medicine master' is the modern word for doctor.

origin: Originally pictured a mound with many people — an army division — then extended to 'master' of a discipline.
culture: 师 honors teachers: 老师 'teacher', 师傅 'master (of a craft)'. Confucius said 'When three walk together, one can be my teacher' (三人行，必有我师).

origin: A phono-semantic compound: 犭(animal radical) marks it as an animal, 苗 gives the sound (and hints at 'meow').
culture: Cats guard Chinese grain stores and hearts alike; the waving 招财猫 'fortune cat' beckons customers at shop entrances. China's real superstar cat is the 熊猫 'bear-cat' — the giant panda.

origin: A phono-semantic compound: 犭(animal radical) plus 句 which gives the sound gǒu — 'dog'.
culture: The Dog is the eleventh zodiac animal, symbol of loyalty. Dogs guard Chinese villages, and 小狗 'little dog' is a fond word for a puppy — though 走狗 'running dog' is an old insult.

origin: A pictograph of a bird with beak, eye, wings and tail feathers.
culture: The bird radical marks feathered words: 鸡 chicken, 鸭 duck, 鹅 goose. Pet songbirds in bamboo cages are a classic sight in Beijing hutongs, taken for 'walks' to the park each morning.
examples: 小鸟 xiǎo niǎo — little bird
花鸟 huāniǎo — flowers and birds (painting genre)

origin: A pictograph of an eye, rotated ninety degrees: the outline is the eye socket, the inner strokes the pupil.
culture: 目 is the eye radical in 眼睛 'eyes'. 目标 'eye's mark' means a goal, and 节目 'section-eye' is a TV program. Chinese has 眉开眼笑 'brows raised, eyes laughing' for a beaming face.

origin: A pictograph of the outer ear with its inner ridges.
culture: The ear radical appears in 听 (traditional 聽, 'to listen with the ear and heart'). Confucius called age sixty 耳顺 'the ear-obeying age' — when one hears truth without offense.

origin: A pictograph of a rice paddy divided into plots by paths and irrigation channels.
culture: Fields fed the empire, so 田 sits at the heart of the writing grid 田字格 — the 'field character grid' every Chinese child uses to center their first characters, and the motif of this app.
examples: 田字格 tiánzìgé — writing practice grid

origin: Three horizontal lines (heaven, man, earth) joined by one vertical stroke — the king who connects all three realms.
culture: 王 'king' doubles as the jade radical 王 (really 玉) in characters like 球 ball, 玩 play, 现在's 现. Jade was the stone of kings, prized above gold.

origin: A pictograph of a standing person with a tattooed or painted chest — 'pattern', then 'writing, culture'.
culture: 文 is culture itself: 文化 'culture', 中文 'Chinese language', 文明 'civilization'. The civil arts 文 were paired with the martial 武 as the twin ideals of the scholar-official.

origin: A pictograph of a person with swinging arms 夭 above a foot 止 — 'to walk, run'.
culture: 走 means both 'walk' and 'leave': 我走了 'I'm off'. 走廊 corridor and 走读 day-student show its range. The 走 radical strides through characters like 起 rise and 越 cross.
examples: 怎么走 zěnme zǒu — how to get there

origin: An ideograph: two people 人 facing each other on the ground 土 — 'to sit'.
culture: 坐 also means 'to take transport': 坐火车 take the train, 坐飞机 fly. Seating order at a Chinese banquet is a fine art — the seat facing the door belongs to the guest of honor.
examples: 坐火车 zuò huǒchē — take the train

origin: A pictograph of nuggets in the earth under a shelter: metal ore — 'gold, metal'.
culture: 金 is one of the five elements and the color of emperors and fortune. The metal radical 钅marks 钱 money, 银 silver, 钢 steel. 金子 gold remains the classic wedding gift.

origin: A pictograph of a curved blade with a handle.
culture: Early Chinese money was cast in knife shapes (刀币). The knife radical 刂cuts through words like 到 arrive and 别 separate. Chinese chefs famously do everything with one cleaver, 菜刀.

origin: A pictograph of a plow — or of a flexed arm with a bulging muscle — 'strength'.
culture: 力 combines into 努力 'to strive' and 力气 'physical strength'. The saying 功夫不负有心人 — 'effort never fails the one with heart' — is every student's motto.
examples: 努力 nǔlì — to work hard

origin: A pictograph of a robe with a collar, lapels and sleeves.
culture: The clothing radical 衤marks 衬衫 shirt and 裤子 pants. Han Chinese traditional dress 汉服 has revived among young people, worn proudly in parks and photo shoots.

origin: A pictograph of a covered food vessel piled high with grain — 'food, to eat'.
culture: The food radical 饣seasons everyday words: 饭 rice, 饮料 drink, 饱 full. 食物 'food', 食堂 'canteen' and the proverb 民以食为天 'the people regard food as heaven' show its weight.

origin: A phono-semantic compound: 亻(person radical) plus 主 which gives the sound — 'where a person stays'.
culture: 住 anchors daily talk: 你住在哪儿？ 'Where do you live?'. Beijing's courtyard homes 四合院 and Fujian's earthen roundhouses 土楼 show how 住 shapes regional culture.
examples: 住在 zhùzài — to live at

origin: An ideograph: a hand 手 held above an eye 目 — shading the eyes to look into the distance.
culture: 看 extends to 看见 'see', 看书 'read' (look at a book) and 看病 'see a doctor' (have one's illness looked at). Tone changes the word: kān 看门 means to guard a door.
examples: 看电影 kàn diànyǐng — watch a movie

origin: The traditional 聽 is a rich ideograph: ear 耳, and components of 'ten eyes one heart' — to listen is to attend with ear, eyes and heart.
culture: Listening 听 is the first skill of Chinese etiquette. 听说 'hear-say' means 'I hear that...' and 听话 'obey' (literally 'listen to words') is what every parent asks of children.
examples: 听说 tīngshuō — to hear of
听音乐 tīng yīnyuè — listen to music

origin: A bamboo 竹 radical over 夭 (a person swaying) — some say bamboo bending in the wind like a laughing body.
culture: 笑 is the laugh of 笑话 jokes and 微笑 smiles. Chinese poetry praises the smile that 笑口常开 'keeps the mouth ever open' — a recipe for long life and good fortune.

origin: A phono-semantic compound: 讠(speech radical) marks it as words, 青 gives the sound — polite speech, 'please, to invite'.
culture: 请 oils every polite exchange: 请问 'may I ask', 请坐 'please sit', 请喝茶 'please have tea'. Removing 请 from a sentence in China is like dropping 'please' in English — instantly brusque.
examples: 请问 qǐngwèn — may I ask
请客 qǐngkè — to treat guests

origin: A phono-semantic compound: 讠(speech) plus 射 which gives the sound — words of gratitude, 'to thank'.
culture: 谢谢 doubled is China's most-used courtesy. Flowers and gratitude share the character family: 谢 also means 'to wither' — classical poets thanked fallen petals. 谢谢 is answered with 不客气 'don't be a guest'.

origin: A pictograph-composite: 雨 (rain) over 彗 (a broom, giving sound) — rain that can be swept: snow.
culture: Snow is a poet's muse: 雪中送炭 'sending charcoal in snowy weather' means timely help. Beijing's first snow fills social media with photos of the vermilion-walled Forbidden City under white.
